title: Halley's Comet Leaves a Trail of Shooting Stars
summary:
You do not have to wait for Halley's Comet to come back to see shooting stars from it. This week, Earth passed through a trail of dust the comet left behind, and the tiny bits made the Orionid meteor shower.

On Oct. 21, photographer Tim McCollum took a special picture above Toccoa, Georgia. Between 3 and 4 in the morning, he caught three bright meteors in the sky. The shooting stars seem to fly out from one point near Betelgeuse, a red giant star in Orion. Halley's Comet is now more than 3 billion miles away, but the dust it shed still glows brightly when it hits our air.

The photo also shows Orion's Belt, the Orion Nebula and the Milky Way. McCollum used a star tracker and joined many photos into one picture.

Missed it? The shower lasts until Nov. 7, so you may still spot a shooting star on a clear night.
why_it_matters: On a clear night before Nov. 7, you can step outside and watch for shooting stars made by dust from a famous comet.

background_read: Halley's Comet is a famous ball of ice and dust that journeys through space and swings past Earth only once in a long while.
As a comet travels, it sheds tiny bits of dust along its path, leaving a long trail floating in space.
When Earth passes through that trail, the dust bits burn up in our air and streak across the sky as shooting stars, and that is what a meteor shower is.
